💬 In plain words   🧭 The chapter as a map   📖 Words to know   🔁 Read it again
This research asks one question — how AI has changed microservice architecture — and answers it under five headings: design, boundaries, communication, operations, and tradeoffs.

Picture a city. A monolith is one department store: everything under one roof, one set of doors, one power supply. Microservices are a street of small shops, each with its own keys, its own till, and its own opening hours, trading with each other across the street. This research asks a precise question: now that AI helps design, build, and run those shops, did the layout of the street change — or only the tools in the builders’ hands?

items.definition: A way of building one application as many small, separately deployable programs (services), each owned by a small team and each with its own data.
Named, reusable solutions to problems that keep recurring — a shared vocabulary, not a library.
The ‘before’ picture that later chapters compare AI’s influence against.
The opposite of microservices: one program, one deployment, one database.

runs.t: The end product is a research article on how AI has changed microservice architecture: design, boundaries, communication, operations, and the tradeoffs that come with those changes.
The work is planned as about two days of deep research, followed by the article written from the evidence gathered.
The history of microservices, and the architectures and design patterns of that style, are the baseline.
Later chapters ask what AI changed in that baseline.
Each answer in the series is saved as its own Word document in this folder, so the draft can be read offline while the research continues.
